Having a higher interest rate to cover one-time administrative fees makes no sense to me :(

Administrative fees are paid up front. Interest is paid on the back end. That's the difference for payday loans - if the borrower had cash to pay administrative fees upfront like you do for a mortgage, they wouldn't be at a payday loan place. And to the immediate counterpoint of "why not backload admin fees", its because that would be no different than interest. People who run into trouble with payday loans arent taking out one loan, they're taking out a succession of loans. And when you take out a succession of loans, admin fees vs interest rates are going to be effectively the same.

And remember that unlike e.g. mortgages, payday loans are unsecured, and really only used by people who're too risky for something as relatively high interest as credit cards. So the risk of default and overhead to chase deadbeats is really high.

if the borrower had cash to pay administrative fees upfront

They just need to take a slightly larger loan and then use some of the cash to pay the administrative fees. Problem solved. That's exactly what you do with mortgages too - you don't actually give them money, they just increase your loan slightly and take the money directly.

Backloading admin fees and interest are effectively the same. I know you're thinking that admin fees would be cheaper, but you misunderstanding how payday loans work. These are ultra short term loans. Two weeks or less is the norm is my understanding. So while admin fees are cheaper for long term loans like a HELOC or mortgage, your mortgage isnt due to be either paid in full or a new one taken out in a matter of weeks. If that were the case, mortgages and HELOCs would have equally high APRs. And the admin fees would end up being similar to high APR because you'd be paying them 26 times a year.

Backloading admin fees and interest are effectively the same.

No they're not. Admin fees are one time thing while interest is repeated. If the loan is of fixed duration then you're right, interest can just be lumped as a known fee. Two weeks or less is the norm is my understanding

Yes and no. Each period is, say, two weeks, but you can "roll over" the loan (call them and ask they extend it by two more weeks). This effectively is as if you took another loan to cover this loan repayment.

So if you do that, you should definitively pay more interest, but why do you have to pay the entire administrative fee again? This barely involves any actual work. They already have your account, you're detailed, they don't need to give you anything. There's no administration involved.
